title: You tested positive. Now what?
hook: The test is 99% accurate. So you're 99% likely to be sick. Right?

knows: that medical tests can be wrong
doesNotKnow: the terms sensitivity, specificity and base rate

misconception: If a test is 99% accurate and you test positive, you are about 99% likely to have the disease (the base rate is ignored).
objective: The learner can explain, by counting a population of 1,000, that when a disease is rare most positive results come from the much larger healthy group, so a positive from an accurate test can still mean a small chance of disease.

claims.text: In this lesson '99% accurate' means the test is positive for 99% of people who have the disease and negative for 99% of people who do not.
claims.source: Sensitivity and specificity, as defined in e.g. Altman & Bland (1994), 'Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity', BMJ 308: 1552.

claims.text: If 1 in 1,000 people has the disease, then among 1,000 people tested we expect about 1 sick person who tests positive and about 10 healthy people who test positive.
claims.source: Expected counts: 1000 x 0.001 x 0.99 = 0.99 true positives; 1000 x 0.999 x 0.01 = 9.99 false positives. Natural-frequency framing: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995), 'How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction', Psychological Review 102(4): 684-704.

claims.text: With a 1-in-1,000 disease and this test, a positive result means about a 9% chance of having the disease.
With the same test, a positive result means about a 50% chance if 1 in 100 people has the disease, and about a 92% chance if 1 in 10 does.
The stage shows the expected counts rounded to whole people, placed at seeded random positions; a real group of 1,000 would vary around these counts.
claims.source: Demo.tsx: counts are round(1000 x prevalence x 0.99) true positives and round(1000 x (1 - prevalence) x 0.01) false positives.

claims.text: In a 1978 study at Harvard Medical School, the most common answer from 60 staff and students to a similar question (1 in 1,000 disease, 5% false-positive rate) was 95%; the correct answer is about 2%.
claims.source: Casscells, Schoenberger & Graboys (1978), 'Interpretation by physicians of clinical laboratory results', New England Journal of Medicine 299: 999-1001.

recall.question: A screening test catches 99% of cases and wrongly flags 1% of healthy people. The condition affects 1 in 10,000. Of the people who test positive, roughly how many have it?
recall.why: Out of 10,000 people, about 1 sick person tests positive, but about 100 healthy people do too. The rarer the condition, the more the healthy group's false alarms swamp the true cases.
